notes.meaning: Jesus looks directly at His astonished followers and explains that saving oneself is impossible for human beings. No person can earn salvation or break free from worldly ties by human willpower alone. God, however, has the power to change human hearts and do what people cannot do for themselves.

differ.view: Salvation is entirely an act of God's sovereign grace, which overcomes human inability and cannot be resisted by those He chooses.

notes.meaning: Peter speaks up to remind Jesus that the disciples walked away from their homes, work, and possessions to follow Him. Unlike the rich ruler who refused to part with his wealth, they really had left everything behind. Peter wonders what this sacrifice will mean for them in the end.

Jesus promises that no one who gives up family or property for His sake and the good news of the gospel will ever be left empty-handed. In this present life, they gain a vast new family of brothers, sisters, and mothers in the church community, along with shelter and support, though these come alongside persecutions. In the world to come, they will receive eternal life, which means living forever in God's presence.

Jesus gives a warning that God's kingdom completely reverses human ideas of importance. Those who enjoy honor and wealth in this world may find themselves last in God's sight, while humble believers who were overlooked will be placed first. It reminds disciples never to boast about what they have given up.

As the group heads up the steep road toward Jerusalem, Jesus walks boldly in front of everyone. His courage and resolve amaze the disciples, while the larger crowd following behind is filled with dread because they know religious leaders want Him dead. Jesus pulls the twelve apostles aside once more to tell them what will soon happen to Him.

Jesus lays out His coming suffering in exact detail for the third time. He tells the Twelve that the Jewish leaders will condemn Him to death and hand Him over to the Roman authorities. The Romans will mock Him, spit on Him, whip Him, and kill Him, but three days later He will rise from the dead.

James and John, the sons of Zebedee, approach Jesus with an open-ended request. They ask Him to promise ahead of time to grant whatever favor they are about to bring up. They act like eager children trying to get a blank check from their teacher.
Jesus does not make a blind promise to the brothers. Instead, He gently asks them to name their request aloud so their motives can be brought into the open.

The two brothers ask to sit at Jesus' right and left sides when He takes His glorious throne. These were the positions of highest rank and power in a royal court. They still pictured the Messiah setting up an earthly political kingdom with top government posts for them.

Jesus tells them that they do not understand what they are asking. The path to His glory goes through deep suffering, which He pictures as drinking a cup of pain and undergoing a baptism of intense sorrow and death.

James and John quickly insist they are able to handle that suffering, not realizing their own human weakness. Jesus tells them they will indeed share in His cup and baptism. James would later be put to death for his faith, and John would face exile and harsh persecution.

Jesus explains that the places of highest honor are not His to hand out as personal favors. Those special positions have already been assigned by God the Father to the people for whom He prepared them.

When the other ten disciples discover what James and John had asked, they become very angry with them. Their frustration grew out of their own ambition, because they also wanted those top spots of honor for themselves.

Jesus gathers all twelve together to address the tension and explain how His kingdom works. In pagan nations, rulers show their greatness by dominating and bossing people around. Jesus warns His followers that they must not copy that worldly style of leadership.

Jesus completely flips the world's definition of greatness upside down. Anyone who wants to become important in His community must be a willing helper to others, and whoever wants the first place must act like a servant to all.

Jesus points to His own life as the ultimate example of true greatness. He did not come to earth to be waited on, but to spend Himself serving others and to give His life as a ransom—a price paid to purchase freedom for captives—to deliver many from sin and death.

differ.view: Christ gave His life as an effectual ransom specifically intended to purchase and secure salvation for the elect.
Christ gave His life as a ransom on behalf of all humanity, making salvation freely available to anyone who believes.

notes.meaning: Jesus and His followers reach the oasis city of Jericho and soon set out with a large crowd of festival travelers. A blind beggar named Bartimaeus sits along the edge of the road, relying on the generosity of passing pilgrims to survive.

As soon as Bartimaeus hears that Jesus from Nazareth is nearby, he begins calling out loudly. He calls Jesus the 'Son of David,' which is a royal title for the promised Messiah, showing his faith that Jesus has the power and mercy to help him.

Many people in the crowd tell the beggar to be quiet, treating him as an annoying disturbance. Instead of staying silent, Bartimaeus shouts all the more desperately for the Son of David to show him mercy.
Jesus stops walking and commands the crowd to bring the man forward. The people immediately cheer the blind man up, telling him to take heart and get to his feet because the Master is asking for him.
Filled with joy and hope, Bartimaeus throws off his heavy outer cloak so nothing can trip him up. He leaps to his feet and hurries through the crowd straight to Jesus.

Jesus asks the blind man what he wants Him to do, giving him room to voice his personal need. Bartimaeus addresses Jesus as 'Rabboni,' a word of deep respect meaning 'my Master,' and simply asks to be given his sight back.

Jesus grants the request at once, telling the man that his faith has healed him and made him whole. Bartimaeus immediately receives his sight and chooses to follow Jesus on the road toward Jerusalem as a thankful disciple.
